newsitem.title: USA: Global M&As hit record $130 million in first half.
newsitem.headline: Global M&As hit record $130 million in first half.

text.p: Global mergers and acquisitions rose to an all-time high of $130 billion in the first half of the year, on track to topple 1996's record, even as prices paid soared 47 percent, KPMG Peat Marwick LLP said Monday.
The figure is 9 percent higher than the $119 billion in the first six months of 1996, according to the accounting and consulting firm's twice-yearly survey.
The average price that companies paid for an acquisition jumped to $56 million from $38 million over the same period.

"When the world's markets are generally healthy and growing, especially financial markets, purchasers take bolder steps. This can mean acquiring instead of partnering," said Steve Blum, a KPMG corporate finance partner based in New York.
"As global competition intensifies and product and service life cycles become shorter, global firms turn to outright acquisitions as a quicker and more impactful solution."
KPMG noted broader global participation in mergers and acquisitions this year, and a shift away from targets in the Pacific Rim and toward Latin America and Western Europe.
The company attributed the longer-term mergers-and-acquisitions- trend to strong global economic and financial environment in 1997.

For the past several years, companies seeking ties across boarders have been increasingly structuring deals as outright acquisitions rather than as joint ventures or strategic alliances, it said. For example, outright acquisitions accounted for 66 percent of cross-border spending from January through June, up from 60 percent in the year-ago period.

U.S. corporations continued to drive global mergers and acquisitions, with a growing emphasis on overseas targets, helped by the strong dollar and the stock market rally. U.S. companies announced $28.1 billion in spending on 683 targets abroad, up 12 percent from $25.0 billion involving 806 targets during the first half of 1996, KPMG said.
However, foreign spending on U.S. targets fell to $26.5 billion on 371 deals, down 25 percent from $35.4 billion in 1996's first half for 441 U.S. targets.

"The United States will probably be the world's favourite target for years to come, because we're the world's largest and most stable consumer and industrial market, but the cost of entry here has gotten a lot steeper lately," Blum said.

The medical field, historically an area where purchasers have stayed close to home, emerged as an important focus for cross-border deals, KPMG said. Several large deals contributed to a midyear mergers-and-acquisitions total of $14.3 billion, almost triple the $5.5 billion in the first half of 1996.
In utilities, spending almost doubled from $6.9 billion to $12 billion as state-owned operations were privatised and the U.S. industry faced deregulation.
Telecommunications was increasingly popular in 1997, with purchasers spending $11.6 billion, up 186 percent from the first half of 1996, KPMG said.

"Continuing waves of deregulation and new technology seem to be disrupting the status quo in these fields, creating consolidation and vertical linkages between strategic players both large and small," said Blum.
Targets in the Pacific Rim, including China, attracted $21.9 billion in 371 announced purchases through the midyear, down from $23.3 billion spent on 657 purchases during the same period last year.
Latin America has emerged to rival the Pacific Rim as a global target, attracting $16.9 billion through midyear, up 160 percent from the first half of 1996, KPMG said.
